football_evidence.question: Can BYU take away Iowa State’s big plays?
football_evidence.assessment: Some measured evidence supports EdgeDesk’s lean toward BYU, and its own breakdown accounts for about 0.2 of the 3.9 points, but not the full gap. It is a research question, not a bet.

When Iowa State has the ball (the line of scrimmage on running plays): Iowa State’s offense is stopped at or behind the line on 21.3% of its runs, and BYU’s defense stops 23.7% of opponent runs at or behind the line (FBS average 17.4%).
When BYU has the ball (the run game against the run defense): BYU’s offense averages 6.5 yards per carry, and Iowa State’s defense allows 5.7 yards per carry (FBS average 5.1).

When BYU has the ball (the line of scrimmage on running plays): BYU’s offense is stopped at or behind the line on 11.6% of its runs, and Iowa State’s defense stops 16.0% of opponent runs at or behind the line (FBS average 17.4%).
contradicting: When Iowa State has the ball (big plays on the ground): Iowa State’s offense turns 10.0% of its runs into explosive gains, and BYU’s defense gives up explosive gains on 5.5% of opponent runs (FBS average 6.6%).
In his last two games (Colorado State and TCU), Bachmeier averaged 7.2 yards per attempt, against 9.0 in his two games before that.
EdgeDesk’s position-group ratings put Iowa State’s running backs No. 25 nationally and BYU’s No. 98.

When Iowa State has the ball (pass protection against the pass rush): Iowa State’s offense has allowed a sack on 3.9% of its dropbacks, and BYU’s defense sacks the quarterback on 6.3% of opponent dropbacks (FBS average 5.6%).

Jaylen Raynor has completed 70 of 120 passes (58.3%) for 903 yards, 7.5 yards per attempt, 6 touchdowns and 3 interceptions in five games for Iowa State, and has been sacked on 5 of 125 dropbacks.
